visuals.title: What a seizure is
nodes: Start focally, or both hemispheres at once

glossary.Unprovoked: Occurring without an immediate trigger such as low glucose, alcohol withdrawal or head injury.
glossary.Generalised tonic-clonic: A seizure involving both hemispheres: loss of consciousness, stiffening, then rhythmic jerking.
glossary.Tonic phase: The stiffening part of a seizure, with sustained muscle contraction.
glossary.Clonic phase: The rhythmic jerking part of a seizure.
glossary.Focal: Starting in one area of one hemisphere of the brain.
glossary.Drop attack: A sudden fall from loss of muscle tone without warning or loss of consciousness.
glossary.Epigastric: Relating to the upper central abdomen; a rising epigastric feeling is a classic temporal lobe aura.
glossary.Temporal lobe: Brain lobe at the side of the head, handling memory, emotion, smell and hearing.
glossary.Frontal lobe: Brain lobe at the front, controlling movement, behaviour and personality.
glossary.Hippocampus: Seahorse-shaped structure in the medial temporal lobe essential for forming new memories.
glossary.Hippocampal: Relating to the hippocampus, the memory-forming structure deep in the temporal lobe.
glossary.Hallucinations: Perceiving something that is not there, such as a smell, sound or sight.
glossary.Complex partial seizures: Older name for focal seizures with impaired awareness.
glossary.Photic stimulation: Flashing lights, used as a seizure trigger in some epilepsies and during EEG.
glossary.Vasovagal syncope: Fainting from a reflex drop in heart rate and blood pressure, with rapid recovery.
glossary.Seizure threshold: How easily the brain can be tipped into a seizure; some drugs lower it.
glossary.Quinolones: Antibiotic class including ciprofloxacin that can lower the seizure threshold.
glossary.Electrolytes: Salts in the blood such as sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium.
glossary.Capillary blood glucose: Finger-prick blood sugar test giving a result in seconds.
glossary.Hypoglycaemia: Low blood glucose, which can itself cause seizures and must be excluded first.
glossary.Hypoxia: Low oxygen levels in the tissues.
glossary.MRI: Magnetic resonance imaging; detailed brain scan used to find a structural cause.
glossary.Gabapentin: Antiepileptic and neuropathic pain drug, a second-line option for focal seizures.
glossary.Lacosamide: Antiepileptic that slowly inactivates sodium channels; second-line for focal seizures.
glossary.Mirena: Brand of levonorgestrel intrauterine system, preferred contraception with enzyme-inducing AEDs.
glossary.Contraception: Methods to prevent pregnancy; enzyme-inducing AEDs make hormonal pills less effective.
glossary.Folic acid: B vitamin given before and in pregnancy (5 mg on AEDs) to reduce neural tube defects.
glossary.Teratogenicity: The ability of a drug to cause birth defects.
glossary.Hirsutism: Excess male-pattern hair growth, a side effect of phenytoin.
glossary.Peripheral neuropathy: Damage to peripheral nerves causing numbness, tingling or weakness, usually in hands and feet.
glossary.Megaloblastic anaemia: Anaemia with large red cells caused by folate or B12 deficiency.
glossary.Bone marrow dysfunction: Reduced production of blood cells by the bone marrow.
glossary.Voltage-gated sodium channels: Membrane channels that open with depolarisation to let sodium in and fire action potentials.
glossary.Convulsive status epilepticus: A tonic-clonic seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures without recovery between.
glossary.PR diazepam: Diazepam given rectally, a pre-hospital option for prolonged seizures.
glossary.ITU: Intensive therapy unit, also called ICU.
glossary.General anaesthesia: Drug-induced unconsciousness, used to stop refractory status epilepticus.
glossary.Pre-eclampsia: Pregnancy disorder after 20 weeks with high blood pressure and proteinuria; seizures mean eclampsia.
glossary.Traumatic brain injury: Brain damage from an external force such as a blow to the head.
glossary.Hypersynchronous: Many neurons firing together at the same moment, abnormally.
glossary.Cortical neurons: Nerve cells in the outer grey matter of the brain.
glossary.Hemispheres: The left and right halves of the brain.
glossary.Chloride influx: Movement of negative chloride ions into a neuron, making it less likely to fire.
glossary.Internalisation: Removal of receptors from the cell surface into the cell, so drugs cannot act on them.
glossary.Benzodiazepines: Sedative drugs (lorazepam, diazepam, midazolam) that enhance GABA-A receptors; first-line for prolonged seizures.
glossary.Psychic aura: Strange feelings such as deja vu, fear or unreality at the start of a seizure.
glossary.Autonomic: Relating to the involuntary nervous system controlling gut, heart and sweating.
